items.title: iv) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Formation of a substance (ΔHf°) using Enthalpy of Combustion and Enthalpies of Formation of other substances

source_refs.note: iv) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Formation of a substance (ΔHf°) using Enthalpy of Combustion and Enthalpies of Formation of other substances: a main subheading of 6.8 Hess's law of heat summation, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 128-128.

blocks.text: Sample problem 6.6 Propane (C₃H₈(g)) burns in oxygen according to the equation:

When 14.64 g of propane is burned in an excess of oxygen in a calorimeter at 25 °C and 1 atm pressure, 678.6 kJ of heat is evolved. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of propane. The standard enthalpies of formation of CO₂(g) and H₂O(g) are –393.51 kJ mol⁻¹ and –241.82 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively.
Solution: The first step is to find the enthalpy change when one mole of propane is burned.
No. of moles of propane = 14.64/44.096 = 0.3320 mol
So, 0.3320 mol propane evolves heat = 678.6 kJ
1.0 mol propane evolves heat = 678.6/0.3320 kJ mol⁻¹ = –2044 kJ mol⁻¹
According to Hess’ law: ΔHr = [3 × ΔH°f (CO₂) + 4 × ΔH°f (H₂O)] – [1 × ΔH°c (C₃H₈) + 5 × ΔH°c (O₂)]
Taking the heat of combustion of O₂(g) to be zero and solving this equation for ΔH°f (C₃H₈) gives,

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the Hess sum the reactant terms are enthalpies of formation, not of combustion: [1 × ΔH°f (C₃H₈) + 5 × ΔH°f (O₂)], and it is the enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) that is zero, because O₂ is an element in its standard state. Solving gives ΔH°f (C₃H₈) = –104 kJ mol⁻¹, as the book finds. The numbering is also a slip: the print has no Sample problem 6.5 and goes from 6.4 to 6.6; nothing is missing, so this is the fifth sample problem.

blocks.prompt: Draw enthalpy cycle of sample problem 6.6 according to Hess’ law to validate above calculation.
blocks.explanation: At the bottom write the elements: 3C(graphite) + 4H₂(g) + 5O₂(g). At the top left write C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) and at the top right 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g). Arrow from the elements to C₃H₈: ΔH°f(C₃H₈) = ?; arrow from the elements to the products: 3(−393.51) + 4(−241.82) = −2147.81 kJ; arrow from C₃H₈ + 5O₂ to the products: ΔHc = −2044 kJ. The two routes are equal: ΔH°f(C₃H₈) + (−2044) = −2147.81, so ΔH°f(C₃H₈) = −104 kJ mol⁻¹.

Green arrow from the elements to propane: ΔH°f(C₃H₈) = ?; red arrow from propane to the products: ΔH°c = −2044 kJ; blue arrow from the elements to the products: 3(−393.51) + 4(−241.82) = −2147.81 kJ. answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: Hess's law enthalpy cycle for Sample problem 6.6 (propane)
answer_figure.long_description: Three boxes: the elements 3C(graphite) + 4H₂(g) + 5O₂(g) at the bottom; C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) at the top left; 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g) at the top right. Route 1 (green + red): the elements first form propane (ΔH°f = ?), then propane burns (ΔH°c = −2044 kJ). Route 2 (blue): the elements form the products directly, 3(−393.51) + 4(−241.82) = −2147.81 kJ. By Hess's law the two routes have the same enthalpy change: ΔH°f + (−2044) = −2147.81, so ΔH°f(C₃H₈) = −104 kJ mol⁻¹, which agrees with the book's calculation.
